newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ENGEN IN 100 MLN RAND TANZANIAN INVESTMENT.
newsitem.headline: ENGEN IN 100 MLN RAND TANZANIAN INVESTMENT.

text.p: Engen Ltd said on Thursday in had invested 100 million rand in a state-of-the-art bulk oil terminal in Tanzania with the pre-emptive right to take over two service station networks.
Chief executive Rob Angel said Engen had also acquired a pre-emptive right to take over two service station networks.
He told a media briefing that the deal included several inland depots, "which will open up the whole hinterland."
"It is a major investment for us," he said.
The tank farm had been bought from an independent trader who had recently bought service station networks from departing multinationals Esso and Caltex.
"He has a deadline by which to covert the Esso brand name and the Caltex brand name into his own brand name," Angel said.
"That will cost money and we have a pre-emptive right on that (in case he ran into difficulties)."
Angel said that Engen had been keen to get into Africa for several years.
"(We have been) putting volumes into Africa since 1990, but now for the first time there is substantial evidence of serious investment going in there."

He attributed this to the fact that Malaysian state-owned oil company Petronas had given Engen a heavy cash injection at the time it took up a 30 percent stake in the South African company earlier this year.

"That makes it easier for us to pursue that activity (moving into Africa) much more aggressively than we could have done before, particularly given our earnings last year when we really had to rein in everything," he said.
He said Engen's market share by volume in Africa north of the Limpopo was now 10 percent but the aim was to take this up to between 20 and 25 percent.
Engen had operations in Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Zaire, Kenya and Tanzania.
On oil exploration subsidiary Energy Africa Ltd , Angel said it had acreage in the right areas. He said the company was having "great success" in offshore Congo, Angola and Namibia.
This, however, was not fully reflected in its share price yet, particularly because many investors ignored the fact that it was a straight rand hedge, Angel said.
